**The CTA now says "run this test yourself".** That's only true if (a)–(e) above work in Qube for a viewer on the free plan.

**The paper's link** is still "to be added" in `claims-and-proof`. A3's CHECK covers the title card, but the row needs the link.

**The two-crowds explanation is still cut** (original lines 9–11). It isn't in `claims-and-proof`. If the paper's own explanation (traders at the open vs at the close) is added there, it can come back as a kept line.
**"So what's actually going on?" is kept** on your direction. The brief listed it under "Don't copy". Your direction wins; flagging it so the brief can be updated.

**Micron with the fee:** at 0.01% on every buy and every sell, Micron still ends at about $368,000 per $1 (`claims-and-proof`, tested by REDPEN). The script never puts the fee on Micron, and the fee result line starts with "The S&P 500".

**Length is about 56s** (180 words, the original is 177). Trimmed in round 3 to the original's word range (`script-logic` #10). The cut words that still matter (the overnight rule, the $14,771 opposite result, the penny-per-$100 fee, 2015–2024) are on screen in the EDIT doc.

lines.text: If you bought Micron every day when the market closed and sold it the next morning when it opened, since 1990, you'd be up over 138 million percent.
Now, imagine you did the exact opposite.
You bought when the market opened and you sold when the market closed.
That same exact trade would be down over 99 percent.
And apparently, Micron isn't the only stock that does this.
A research paper found the same phenomenon across hundreds of stocks.
So what's actually going on?
There's two different crowds trading at two different times.
Regular people tend to trade around market open, reacting to whatever news came out overnight.
Big institutions trade during the day and into close because that's where liquidity is.
And the research says that the biggest portions of stock returns actually happen while the market is closed.
So if you're only trading between open and close, you might be missing the entire point.
And if you want to see my entire portfolio for completely free common stocks, then I'll send it over to you.
